mnemonics.title: Memory aids cheat sheet
mnemonics.content:
Malware removal order — "Verify, Quarantine, Disable, Remediate, Schedule, Enable, Educate"

Very Quick Dogs Run So Everyone Escapes.

Wireless security strength (weak → strong)

WEP < WPA (TKIP) < WPA2 (AES/CCMP) < WPA3 (SAE). Always pick the highest the question allows.

"Something you…" factors (MFA)

  • Know — password, PIN, security question
  • Have — phone, token, smart card
  • Are — fingerprint, face, retina
  • Somewhere you are — GPS/geolocation; Something you do — gesture/behavior

True MFA combines factors from different categories. Two passwords is not MFA.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting methodology (memorize this)
troubleshooting.content:
CompTIA tests the order of these steps directly. If a question asks "what should the technician do first/next," map the scenario onto this list.

Best-practice methodology — 6 steps

  1. Identify the problem. Gather information from the user, identify symptoms, ask about changes, duplicate the problem if possible. Always back up before making changes.
  2. Establish a theory of probable cause — question the obvious. Consider the simplest explanation first.
  3. Test the theory to determine the cause. If confirmed, move on. If not, establish a new theory or escalate.
  4. Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and implement the solution. Refer to vendor docs.
  5. Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures.
  6. Document findings, actions, and outcomes.

For the exam: "Question the obvious" lives in step 2. "Back up" happens during step 1, before any change. Documentation is always last.

1.1.title: Operating-system basics
1.1.content:
OS / editionWhy it shows up on the exam
Windows 10/11 HomeConsumer edition — cannot join a Windows domain and lacks BitLocker.
Windows 10/11 ProThe minimum edition to join a domain and use BitLocker. Enterprise / Education also qualify.
macOSApple's desktop OS. Default file system is APFS (snapshots, encryption, journaling).
LinuxOpen-source. Dominates web servers and embedded systems.
Chrome OSBrowser-centric, Google-managed; common in education.

End-of-life (EOL)

EOL = the vendor stops supporting the OS. No more security updates. Continuing to run an EOL OS in production is a compliance and security problem; plan migrations before the date.

For the exam: Windows Home → no domain, no BitLocker. APFS = Mac. EOL = no patches.

1.2.title: Windows command-line tools
1.2.content:
CommandWhat it does
ipconfigShow/refresh IP config. /all shows MAC + DNS; /release + /renew for DHCP; /flushdns clears resolver cache.
pingTest reachability via ICMP. ping -t runs continuously.
netstatActive connections + listening ports. -a all, -n numeric, -b owning process.
nslookupQuery DNS records for a host.
tracertTrace the router hops to a destination.
sfc /scannowSystem File Checker — repairs corrupt Windows system files.
chkdskCheck disk. /f fixes errors, /r recovers bad sectors (schedules at reboot for the system drive).
dismServicing of the Windows image; /RestoreHealth repairs the component store that sfc relies on.
diskpartScriptable partition/volume management.
gpupdate / gpresultForce a Group Policy refresh / show the resulting policy set.
taskkillEnd a process by PID or image name.
shutdown/r restart, /s shutdown, /t delay.
winverShow the Windows edition + build number.

For the exam: if files are corrupt, run sfc /scannow; if sfc can't fix them, run dism … /RestoreHealth first, then sfc again.

1.3.title: Windows OS tools
1.3.content:
ToolUse for
Local Users and Groups (lusrmgr.msc)Rename / disable / change accounts on a standalone Windows desktop.
Device Manager (devmgmt.msc)Driver issues — disabled devices, missing drivers, hardware not responding (e.g. dead touchpad).
Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc)System / Application / Security logs — diagnose BSODs, intermittent errors, audit failures.
Services (services.msc)Start / stop / configure services (print spooler, Windows Update, etc.).
File Explorer OptionsShow file extensions, show hidden files. Hidden extensions cause confusion when renaming (e.g. document.txt → document.xml looks renamed but really is document.xml.txt).
Task SchedulerRun scripts / programs on a schedule or trigger.
Disk ManagementPartition, format, assign drive letters.

Windows 11 hardware requirement

TPM 2.0 is mandatory for installing or upgrading to Windows 11 — alongside UEFI + Secure Boot. A failed Win 10 → Win 11 upgrade on otherwise modern hardware almost always means missing/disabled TPM.

For the exam: match the tool to the symptom (drivers → Device Manager; logs → Event Viewer; services → services.msc). Win 11 needs TPM 2.0.

1.4.title: Windows Settings & Control Panel
1.4.content:
The exam quizzes you on where in Windows a setting lives — Settings vs Control Panel vs Task Manager vs Registry Editor.

SettingWhere
Speech recognition, Narrator, Magnifier, large textEase of Access
Add / remove accounts; allow Remote Desktop multi-userUser Accounts
Silence pop-ups during a meetingDo Not Disturb / Focus Assist in Notification settings
Edit HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE directlyRegistry Editor (regedit.exe)
Disable startup programsTask Manager → Startup tab
Live per-process CPU / disk / memory / networkResource Monitor (resmon.exe)
Camera / microphone / location app permissionsSettings → Privacy

For the exam: "interactive registry edit" → regedit. "Slow because of paging" → Resource Monitor. "App permissions" → Privacy.

1.5.title: Windows networking & system commands
1.5.content:
NeedTool / command
Set a different audio output deviceSound settings → set as default audio device
Show hidden files / file extensionsFile Explorer Options
Rebuild the boot configuration databasebootrec /rebuildbcd (related: /fixmbr, /fixboot)
Repair corrupt Windows system filessfc /scannow (run dism … /RestoreHealth first if SFC can't repair)
Clear the DNS resolver cacheipconfig /flushdns
Newly installed app broke a previously-working local portWindows Defender Firewall — the install probably added/blocked a rule

For the exam: "no boot device after a tweak" → bootrec. "Out-of-date DNS" → ipconfig /flushdns. "App X breaks port Y on this PC only" → host firewall.

1.6.title: Windows networking setup
1.6.content:
• DNS for domain join — workstations need to find the domain controller via DNS. "Cannot locate the domain" → set DNS server to the DC.
  • Static IP from help desk — usually because DHCP isn't enabled on that subnet, so each device must be configured manually.
  • Roaming profiles — user's desktop, settings, and files follow them across any domain-joined workstation. Right answer when "users work at different PCs" and need a consistent environment.
  • Captive portal — public Wi-Fi (hotel, airport, café) that pops a sign-in / terms page. Connect, read the pop-up, accept. Wi-Fi only works after that.
  • Accessibility (Ease of Access) — Narrator, Magnifier, larger text, high contrast.
  • Privacy — per-app camera / microphone / location permissions.

For the exam: "domain not found" → check DNS. "Wi-Fi connected but no internet at airport" → captive portal. "Same profile on any computer" → roaming profiles.

1.7.title: Applications & services
1.7.content:
• "Turn Windows features on or off" — install/enable optional components like .NET Framework, IIS, Hyper-V, WSL.
  • License device limit — SaaS / subscription apps can refuse installs once you hit the seats you've paid for. Symptom: "the install is unavailable due to license."
  • Shared cloud doc not working — verify viewing and sharing permissions on the link; "Anyone with the link can edit" vs "view only" vs domain-restricted.
  • UNC path syntax — \\server\share\path. Double backslash leads, single backslash separates.
  • Network profile — pick Public on untrusted networks; Windows Defender Firewall locks down inbound connections. Private = home / trusted network, looser rules.
  • Proxy auto-config — if the network requires a proxy and there's no PAC file, you must enter the proxy IP and TCP port manually.

For the exam: ".NET missing" → Turn Windows features on/off. "Locked down inbound for café Wi-Fi" → Public profile.

1.8.title: File systems
1.8.content:
File systemUse / notes
NTFSWindows default. Journaling, file/folder permissions, EFS encryption, compression, quotas, large volumes & files. Required to join a domain.
FAT32Highly compatible across OSes, but 4 GB max file size and 2 TB partition limit. No permissions.
exFATDesigned for flash/SD media. Handles >4 GB files; read/write on Windows and macOS. No journaling.
ext3 / ext4Linux file systems; ext4 is the modern journaling default.
APFSModern macOS default — snapshots, cloning, encryption.
HFS+Older macOS ("Mac OS Extended").

For the exam: a USB drive that must hold a 6 GB file and work on both Mac and Windows → exFAT. Need file-level permissions/encryption on Windows → NTFS.

1.9.title: OS installation & Linux basics
1.9.content:
Deployment methods (large-scale installs)

  • PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) — the workstation boots from the NIC, fetches a deployment image over the network. Standard for "image hundreds of machines on first power-on."
  • Network-based deployment with a tool like MDT/SCCM/Intune is the right answer for many devices, mixed hardware vendors, multiple images.
  • In-place upgrade — fastest path from Windows 10 to 11 without losing data, apps, or settings.
  • Clean install / repair install / recovery partition / image deployment / remote / unattended (answer file) are the other install types worth recognizing.

32-bit vs 64-bit; partition styles

  • The deciding factor for 32 vs 64-bit is installed RAM — 32-bit Windows can address only ≈ 4 GB; if Windows reports 4 GB on a 16 GB box, you're on a 32-bit edition.
  • MBR: ≤ 2 TB partitions, max 4 primary partitions, legacy BIOS.
  • GPT: needed for > 2 TB partitions or > 4 primary partitions, paired with UEFI. Windows 11 requires GPT/UEFI + Secure Boot + TPM 2.0 — failed upgrade is usually the missing TPM.

Multi-boot & cross-OS gotchas

  • For Windows + Linux on one box, install Windows first — Windows setup overwrites the bootloader; GRUB can include Windows but not the other way around.
  • Moving a USB drive between Windows and Linux/macOS → format exFAT (or FAT32 if files are < 4 GB).

Linux survival commands

CommandWhat it does
ls / pwd / cdList / show / change directory.
cp / mv / rmCopy / move / remove. rm -rf deletes recursively without prompting.
chmod / chownChange permission bits / change owner or group.
findSearch for files/directories by name, type, size, etc.
grepSearch for patterns inside files.
ps / top / killList processes / live monitor / terminate by PID.
apt (Debian/Ubuntu) / dnf or yum (Red Hat/Fedora)Install, update, remove packages.
sudo / suRun a single command as another user (usually root) / switch user.
manRead the manual page for a command.

For the exam: "many computers, image at first boot" → PXE. Windows 11 upgrade fails on perfectly modern hardware → TPM. Linux package manager differs by distro family.

1.10.title: Installing & deploying applications
1.10.content:
Installer types by OS

ExtensionOS
.msi / .exeWindows. MSI uses Windows Installer; both usually need administrator privileges to write to Program Files / the registry.
.dmg / .pkg / .appmacOS. A .dmg is a mountable disk image you drag the app from.
.apkAndroid. Sideloading one outside the Play Store requires enabling "install unknown apps".
.deb / .rpmLinux (Debian / Red Hat families).

Before installing — check requirements

  • Hardware — CPU, RAM, free disk, and sometimes a specific GPU (an "RTX features not supported" error = the graphics adapter doesn't meet minimums).
  • OS compatibility — edition and version (32- vs 64-bit).
  • Permissions — admin rights for system-wide installs; impact on the network/other users for shared machines.

For the exam: a .dmg is always macOS; sideloading Android apps means enabling unknown sources.

1.11.title: Common OS / cloud concepts
1.11.content:
Cloud service models

  • SaaS — finished software you just use (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Dropbox).
  • PaaS — a platform to build/deploy apps on (runtime, DB, no server management).
  • IaaS — raw virtual infrastructure (VMs, storage, networking) you manage.

Identity & sync

  • Identity synchronization (e.g. on-prem Active Directory ↔ Entra ID) gives single sign-on — one set of credentials for local and cloud resources.
  • File-sync status icons (OneDrive): a green check = fully synced to the cloud; spinning arrows = sync in progress.

Linux permissions quickie

chmod uses octal: 4 = read, 2 = write, 1 = execute, summed per owner/group/other. So chmod 750 = owner rwx (7), group r-x (5), others none (0).

For the exam: productivity suites in the browser = SaaS. One login for local + cloud = identity sync / SSO.

2.1.title: Security concepts: authentication, MFA & physical security
2.1.content:
Authentication & MFA

  • True multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories: something you know (password, PIN), have (phone, smart card, token), are (fingerprint, face, retina), plus somewhere you are (GPS) and something you do (behavior).
  • Smart card + fingerprint = MFA (have + are). Password + PIN = not MFA (both "know").
  • Authenticator apps (push approve/deny notifications) and TOTP codes are common second factors. A symptom of "MFA suddenly broken after travel" is usually a clock / time-zone mismatch on the device generating TOTP codes.
  • Hashing (one-way function) is how stored passwords are protected — never reversible to plaintext.

Access control models / principles

  • Principle of least privilege — users get the minimum access required for their role.
  • Implicit deny — anything not explicitly permitted is automatically refused.
  • Zero Trust — never trust, always verify. Continuously authenticate, authorize, and validate every user, device, and session, inside or outside the network.
  • RBAC (role-based), MAC (mandatory, labels), DAC (discretionary, owner sets).

Physical security controls

ControlWhat it does
Access control vestibule / mantrapTwo interlocking doors; the outer must close before the inner opens. Defeats tailgating.
BollardsReinforced posts that block vehicle ramming.
Cameras / surveillanceDetects and documents entry into restricted areas — primarily a detective control.
Badge readers, biometricsAuthenticate the person at the door.
Cable lockTethers a laptop to a desk against grab-and-go theft.
EncryptionRenders data unreadable on a lost/stolen device — a logical control, not physical, but worth pairing here.

For the exam: "two different factor categories" = MFA. Cameras don't prevent, they detect/document. Bollards stop vehicles, mantraps stop tailgaters.

2.2.title: Wireless security
2.2.content:
ProtocolEncryptionVerdict
WEPRC4Broken — never use.
WPATKIPDeprecated.
WPA2AES / CCMPStrong; still common.
WPA3AES + SAEStrongest; forward secrecy, protects weak passwords.

Personal vs Enterprise

  • Personal (PSK) — one shared passphrase for everyone.
  • Enterprise (802.1X) — each user authenticates against a RADIUS server with their own credentials.

For the exam: pick the strongest protocol the scenario supports. AES is the modern cipher; TKIP and WEP are red flags.

2.3.title: Malware types & enterprise auth
2.3.content:
TypeWhat it does
VirusAttaches to a host file; needs user execution to spread.
WormSelf-propagates over the network; no host file needed.
TrojanLooks legit, hides malicious functionality. Remote Access Trojan (RAT) opens a back door.
RansomwareEncrypts files, demands payment (often crypto) for the decryption key.
RootkitHides at a low level (kernel / boot) to evade detection.
Keylogger / spywareCaptures keystrokes or activity silently.
Fileless malwareUses the host's native scripting environment (e.g. PowerShell) to run in memory. Hard to detect because there's no malicious file on disk.
PUP (potentially unwanted program)Bundled extra software in a legitimate installer. Not technically malware, but unwanted.
CryptominerUses the victim's CPU / GPU to mine cryptocurrency.

Enterprise auth protocols (also tested here)

  • WPA3 / SAE — replaces the WPA2 4-way handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals; resists offline dictionary attacks.
  • RADIUS — authenticates user / device access to networks (Wi-Fi 802.1X, VPN).
  • TACACS+ — primarily for administrative access to network devices (routers, switches). Cisco-origin.
  • Kerberos — Windows-domain authentication (ticket-based).

For the exam: "uses PowerShell to run in memory" → fileless. "Admin login to a router" → TACACS+. "WPA3's handshake" → SAE.

2.4.title: Social engineering, threats & vulnerabilities
2.4.content:
Social engineering

  • Phishing (email) → spear phishing (targeted) → whaling (executives). Vishing = voice, smishing = SMS.
  • Shoulder surfing — watching you type. Tailgating / piggybacking — following someone through a secure door.
  • Dumpster diving — harvesting discarded info. Impersonation / pretexting — pretending to be someone trusted.
  • Evil twin — rogue AP mimicking a legit SSID.

Attacks

  • DoS / DDoS — exhaust a resource so it's unavailable (DDoS = many sources / botnet).
  • On-path (formerly man-in-the-middle) — attacker relays/alters traffic between two parties.
  • Brute force tries every combination; dictionary uses a wordlist.
  • Zero-day — exploit for a vulnerability with no vendor patch yet.
  • Spoofing — forging an identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID).

For the exam: match the delivery channel to the term — a fraudulent text is smishing, a fraudulent call is vishing.

2.5.title: Wireless attacks, web attacks & policy
2.5.content:
• Evil twin — rogue Wi-Fi AP using a legit SSID (coffee shop, hotel) to intercept traffic.
  • SQL injection (SQLi) — malicious code in a web input field that the database executes (e.g. ' OR 1=1 --). Defense: parameterized queries / prepared statements.
  • Cross-site scripting (XSS) — injects JavaScript that runs in another user's browser session.
  • Smishing — SMS phishing. Vishing — voice phishing. Both are social engineering deliveries.

Windows enforcement tools

  • Group Policy (gpedit / GPO) — push settings across domain-joined machines (e.g. disable Guest, force lock timeout, restrict installs).
  • User Account Control (UAC) — prompts for consent / admin creds before privileged actions. Don't disable to make life "easier"; it's a real defense.
  • BitLocker — full-disk encryption. Protects data when a laptop is lost or stolen even if the drive is removed.

For the exam: "fake AP with the real SSID" → evil twin. "Disable guest on every domain PC at once" → Group Policy. "Stolen laptop, drive is unreadable" → BitLocker.

2.6.title: Securing & hardening workstations
2.6.content:
Account & permission hygiene

  • Principle of least privilege — users don't get admin rights unless they need them. Symptom of violation: apps showing up that weren't installed by default.
  • Disable Guest / rename default Administrator; require strong passwords + lockout policy.
  • BIOS / UEFI password — prevents non-admins from changing firmware settings like enabling virtualization or disabling Secure Boot.
  • MDM (Mobile Device Management) — central control of phones / tablets: enforce passcode, push apps, block unapproved installs, remote wipe.

Encryption at rest

  • BitLocker — full-drive encryption for the internal disk.
  • BitLocker To Go — same idea, for removable USB drives. Trains your staff: encrypt the thumb drive, don't trust "I'll be careful."

Onboarding / offboarding checklist (common offboarding tasks)

  • Deactivate badge / fob / smart-card door access.
  • Disable or transfer the user's account; suspend email.
  • Recover hardware (laptop, phone, tokens).
  • Re-assign their shared resources / project files.

For the exam: "lots of unauthorized installs" → least privilege violation. "Enable VT only by admins" → BIOS password. "Lost USB stick with files" → BitLocker To Go.

2.7.title: Securing & hardening workstations
2.7.content:
Host-hardening techniques

  • Execution control / application allow-listing — only approved programs can run, blocking malware regardless of what the user clicks. (Deny-listing blocks known-bad; allow-listing is stronger.)
  • Disable unused/default accounts — turn off the built-in Guest account and rename/disable default admin accounts.
  • Strong password policy, account lockout, least-privilege user accounts.
  • Patch/update the OS and apps; remove unnecessary software and services.
  • Endpoint protection — anti-malware, host firewall.

Physical / end-user practices

  • Screensaver lock (and lock-on-walk-away) stops shoulder-level access to an unattended workstation.
  • Mantrap / access control vestibule — two interlocking doors where the first must close before the second opens; defeats tailgating.

For the exam: "block software no matter what the user does" → execution control / allow-listing. "Unattended workstation" → screensaver/lock.

2.8.title: Mobile device hardening & data destruction
2.8.content:
Mobile security

  • Biometric screen lock — fingerprint or face. Faster + harder to shoulder-surf than a PIN.
  • Remote wipe — issue via MDM when a device is lost or stolen. Wipes corporate AND personal data.
  • Enterprise wipe — softer alternative: removes corporate accounts and data only, leaves personal data alone. Used on BYOD devices at offboarding.

Data destruction methods (drive disposal)

MethodWhat / when
Low-level formatOverwrites every sector. Drive is reusable afterward.
Crypto-eraseFor self-encrypting drives (SEDs): instantly sanitizes by destroying the encryption key. Fastest method for SEDs.
DegaussingPowerful magnet randomizes the magnetic platters on an HDD. Renders the drive inoperable. No effect on SSDs.
Shredding / drilling / incinerationPhysical destruction. Most certain for SSDs (since they're not magnetic).
Certificate of destructionDocument a third-party disposal vendor must provide to prove the drives were destroyed.

For the exam: "SED quick wipe" → crypto-erase. "HDD made unreadable but recyclable" → degauss. "SSD permanently destroyed" → shred / drill.

2.9.title: SOHO router security & physical drive disposal
2.9.content:
SOHO router settings

  • Port forwarding — maps an external port to an internal IP/port so outside traffic can reach a specific internal host (e.g. a surveillance system's web UI from the LAN/WAN).
  • UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) — lets apps and devices automatically open ports on the router. Disable — it's a documented security risk; malware uses it to expose internal services.
  • DMZ / screened subnet — puts a single host outside the LAN firewall, fully exposed. Last-resort placement for a server that must be wide-open; use only when port forwarding can't do the job.
  • Change the default admin password, update firmware, disable WAN management, use WPA3 (or WPA2 AES at minimum).

Physical destruction (recap)

  • Degaussing = magnetic field, HDD only.
  • Shredding = chips down to small fragments. Works on SSDs and HDDs.
  • Certificate of destruction from the vendor is your audit trail.

For the exam: "expose a single host wide-open" → DMZ. "Self-opening firewall ports" → UPnP — turn it off. "Proof the drive was destroyed" → certificate of destruction.

2.10.title: Browser security & SOHO recap
2.10.content:
• Private / incognito browsing — fixes SSO / cookie session conflicts (e.g. signed into two tenants in the same browser). Also no local history / cookies / cache.
  • Content filtering — proxy or secure web gateway that classifies sites by category and blocks unauthorized ones. Right answer for "policy prevents browsing X category."
  • Internet Options — clear cached images so old versions stop appearing.
  • Extensions / add-ons — install only from official browser stores. Plugin that hooks one-time password prompts = use with caution; password-manager extensions are the legit use case.
  • Certificate warning + no padlock = invalid or untrusted certificate. Don't proceed; this is how on-path attacks present.
  • UPnP on a SOHO router — disable. (Repeated from 2.9 because the exam tests it from this angle too.)

For the exam: "blocked website categories" → content filtering. "Stale page contents" → clear cache via Internet Options. "Padlock missing on https://" → don't trust it.

2.11.title: Browser security
2.11.content:
• Private / incognito mode — doesn't save local history, cookies, or temporary files for that session. (It does not make you anonymous to the network or sites.)
  • Valid certificate + padlock — how a user visually confirms the connection is encrypted (HTTPS) and the site's identity is trusted. A certificate warning means don't proceed.
  • Trusted sources for extensions — install add-ons only from the official browser store; rogue extensions are a common malware vector.
  • Ad / pop-up blockers — reduce intrusive ads and a malvertising attack surface.
  • Password manager, secure settings sync, and clearing cached data round out browser hygiene.

For the exam: padlock + valid certificate = encrypted & trusted; private mode = no local trace, not anonymity.

3.1.title: Windows OS troubleshooting (the biggest objective)
3.1.content:
OBJ 3.1 carries 24 questions in this bank — the single largest. The questions test which tool matches which symptom.

Tool selection by symptom

SymptomGo-to tool
App runs gradually slower; identify which resource is being consumedResource Monitor — granular per-process CPU/disk/network/memory views.
Diagnose BSODs, intermittent service failures, app/system errorsEvent Viewer — System / Application / Security logs.
A service won't start or keeps restarting (e.g. print spooler)Services console (services.msc) — start/stop/restart, recovery actions.
System is 97% memory-bound; everything else idleClose unnecessary programs, then look at adding RAM. Task Manager → Memory.
BSOD right after a new device installFaulty or incompatible driver — roll back or boot to Safe Mode.
Slow desktop load right after sign-inCorrupt user profile — investigate NTUSER.DAT; create a new profile and migrate.

Boot & startup failures

  • "OS not found" / "Boot device not found" — first, verify boot device priority in UEFI/BIOS. Then look at cabling and the disk itself.
  • After a fresh install, "no boot device" → check UEFI boot order and reseat the SATA cable.
  • After a disk-optimization tool corrupts the boot record → boot installation media → use bootrec (/fixmbr, /fixboot, /rebuildbcd) to repair.

Field-tech etiquette wrapped into a question

When you can fix something remotely, do that first rather than dispatching — it's less disruptive and faster.

For the exam: match the diagnostic tool to the symptom — Event Viewer for "intermittent / after the fact," Resource Monitor for "live, per-process," Services console for "service won't start."

3.2.title: PC + mobile security symptoms
3.2.content:
SymptomLikely cause
Personal files renamed; system files missing; performance tanksMalware infection — run anti-malware in Safe Mode after isolating.
Bank URL keeps redirecting to a spoof siteBrowser redirection — malicious extension, hosts-file edit, or DNS hijack. Inspect installed extensions and %SystemRoot%\System32\drivers\etc\hosts.
Persistent pop-up "your computer is severely infected, pay now"Fake security warning (scareware) — close the tab without clicking; it's social engineering.
HTTPS site shows untrusted-certificate warningCould be an on-path attack intercepting traffic. Don't bypass; verify on a known-good network.
Mobile app install keeps failingCheck storage space and that the OS version meets the app's minimum.
Mobile battery drains even when idleInspect Settings → Battery for the worst-offending background apps.

For the exam: "scary pop-up demanding payment" → scareware, never call the number. "Cert warning on a familiar site" → suspect on-path / DNS issue.

3.3.title: Malware removal — best-practice procedure
3.3.content:
This 7-step order is tested directly. Memorize the sequence.

  1. Investigate and verify malware symptoms.
  2. Quarantine the infected systems (disconnect from the network).
  3. Disable System Restore in Windows (so you don't restore an infected snapshot).
  4. Remediate: update anti-malware definitions, then scan and remove — use Safe Mode or a pre-installation environment if needed.
  5. Schedule scans and run updates.
  6. Re-enable System Restore and create a fresh restore point.
  7. Educate the end user to prevent reinfection.

Common malware types

  • Ransomware encrypts data for payment. Trojan hides in a legit-looking program. Rootkit hides at a low level (boot/kernel). Keylogger captures keystrokes. Spyware harvests activity. Worm self-propagates with no host file.

For the exam: quarantine and disabling System Restore come before scanning; educating the user is last.

3.4.title: Mobile OS & connectivity troubleshooting
3.4.content:
SymptomFirst fix to try
Corporate email app won't open after OS upgradeUpdate the app (the old build may be incompatible with the new OS).
Phone needs charging mid-day even though fully charged overnightLook at background apps — disable or restrict the high-use ones.
HD video on a streaming site fails with timeoutInsufficient bandwidth — connectivity issue, not the phone.
Can't get email in a crowded venue (music festival)Too many devices on the same cell / Wi-Fi — wait or move.
Quick discharge after replacing a 2-week-old phoneCheck the per-app battery usage chart for the worst offender.
App install repeatedly fails on AndroidVerify sufficient storage; clear cache; reinstall the Play Store version.
Slow performanceClose background apps; clear cache; restart; check storage.
OverheatingClose GPU-heavy apps; remove the case; stop charging while in use; check for runaway background processes.

For the exam: always isolate "app vs OS vs network." Battery problems → look at the per-app battery usage screen first.

3.5.title: Mobile security troubleshooting
3.5.content:
• Lost phone → Remote wipe (issued via MDM or the carrier / account). Protects corporate data and personal data on a stolen device.
  • Jailbreaking (iOS) / rooting (Android) — gains administrative privileges. Disables built-in security features, voids warranty, and compromises the device's integrity. Don't deploy to a managed fleet.
  • Sudden data overage with no user-driven usage — suspect a malicious app exfiltrating data or doing background cryptomining. Audit installed apps and per-app data usage.
  • Sideloading from third-party sources — bypasses store vetting; high risk of Trojan malware. Disable "install unknown apps" except for one-off trusted installs.
  • App requesting weird permissions — a flashlight asking for GPS / location = likely rogue. Revoke or uninstall.

For the exam: "phone lost / stolen" → remote wipe. "App asks for permissions it has no business needing" → suspect / revoke. "Mystery data usage spike" → malicious app.

4.1.title: Documentation & change management
4.1.content:
• SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) — documented steps for repeatable tasks. "Set up a new employee's accounts" follows an SOP and is logged as a request in the ticketing system (not an incident).
  • Incident = unplanned interruption or degradation (outage, BSOD storm). Request = routine, SOP-covered task (account setup, password reset).
  • Incident report — written summary of an outage: timeline, root cause, actions taken, follow-up.
  • Procurement life cycle — the full lifecycle of an asset from purchase → deployment → maintenance → disposal.
  • CMDB (Configuration Management Database) — central record of hardware, software, and their dependencies. "What service does Server X support?" lives here.
  • Knowledge base — searchable repository of fixes / how-tos. Ticket resolutions feed it; tier-1 staff consult it before escalating.

For the exam: "routine task with known steps" → request, not incident. "Outage write-up" → incident report. "Tracks hardware and dependencies" → CMDB.

4.2.title: Change management
4.2.content:
Formal change management reduces the risk that a "quick fix" breaks production.

  • Documented business processes + a request form describing purpose and scope.
  • Risk analysis and a risk level for the change.
  • Change board approval — the CAB authorizes the change.
  • End-user acceptance before rollout.
  • Sandbox testing in a non-production environment.
  • Rollback / backout plan if the change fails.

For the exam: a documented rollback plan is the safety net — expect a question where the right answer is "ensure there is a way to revert."

4.3.title: Backup & recovery
4.3.content:
The 3-2-1 rule (memorize)

3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of media, with 1 copy stored offline and offsite. Defends against natural disasters, localized hardware failure, and ransomware (which can encrypt online backups too).

Backup methods

MethodWhat's backed upStorageRestore complexity
FullEverything, every timeMostSimplest — restore one set
IncrementalChanges since the last backup (of any type)LeastMost complex — restore the last full + every incremental since
DifferentialChanges since the last full backupMiddleRestore last full + the most recent differential (only two sets)
Synthetic fullServer combines incrementals into a virtual full backupMiddleRestore as if it were a full

Recovery

  • Alternative location recovery — restore to a different site / facility (cloud, secondary data center) when primary infrastructure is destroyed (e.g. after ransomware levels the original servers).

For the exam: "smallest daily backups, hardest restore" → incremental. "Two sets to restore" → differential. "Offline + offsite" → the "1" in 3-2-1.

4.4.title: Safety procedures (electrostatic, lifting, high voltage)
4.4.content:
ESD (electrostatic discharge)

  • Anti-static wrist strap — alligator clip attaches to an unpainted part of the computer's metal chassis (or a grounding plug). NOT to the AC ground while plugged in.
  • Anti-static bags + anti-static mat for storing and working with components (RAM, motherboards).
  • Never wear an ESD strap when working on high-voltage equipment (monitors, PSUs, laser printers' fuser) — the strap tethers you to the device and increases the risk of a lethal shock.

Power supplies, CRT monitors, UPS

  • Do not open a PC power supply. The capacitors retain dangerous voltages for hours after power is removed.
  • Same for older CRT monitors.
  • UPS battery replacement: power off first, but treat the unit as potentially energized.

Lifting & physical safety

  • Use proper lifting technique — bend at the knees, keep the back straight, get help for heavy rack equipment.
  • Cable management to prevent trip hazards.

For the exam: wrist-strap clip = bare metal chassis. PSU and CRT = never open. Inside a microwave / laser-printer fuser = don't wear ESD strap.

4.5.title: Environmental controls (MSDS, toner, power)
4.5.content:
• MSDS / SDS (Material Safety Data Sheet) — vendor document with hazard info, spill cleanup, PPE, disposal. Mandatory reference for chemical spills (UPS battery acid, toner, cleaning chemicals).
  • Toner spills — do not blow compressed air on them; it aerosolizes the fine particles into a respiratory hazard. Use a toner-rated vacuum or damp cloth per the MSDS.
  • Compressed air for dust — use in a well-ventilated area so blown-out dust doesn't recirculate.
  • UPS (uninterruptible power supply) — battery backup that keeps systems running through short blackouts and allows a graceful shutdown.
  • Surge suppressor — clamps voltage spikes. NOT a substitute for a UPS.
  • HVAC / temperature & humidity control in server rooms — too dry = static, too humid = condensation.

For the exam: "where do I find spill cleanup info?" → MSDS. "Server room blackout for 90 seconds" → UPS. "Toner cleanup" → not compressed air.

4.6.title: Privacy, regulated data, AI & forensics
4.6.content:
• EULA / license agreement — controls how you can use software. Features locked behind a corporate login = a license / activation issue, not a bug.
  • AUP (Acceptable Use Policy) — written rules about how employees may use company resources (web, email, AI tools).
  • AI hallucination — model outputs confident, factually wrong information (fake citations, made-up steps). Always verify AI-generated work against authoritative sources before using it.
  • Don't paste sensitive corporate data into public AI tools — the provider may use your input for training, leaking it to others.

Forensics

  • Order of volatility — collect the most volatile evidence first. CPU cache and registers → RAM → routing/ARP tables → disk → archival media. Memory contents disappear on power-off; disks survive.
  • Chain of custody — documented, unbroken record of who handled the evidence, when, and why. Required for evidence to be admissible.

Regulated data categories

  • PII (personally identifiable info), PCI (cardholder data), PHI (health info / HIPAA), GDPR (EU personal data).

For the exam: confidently-wrong AI output = hallucination. "Most volatile first" = CPU / RAM before disk. Evidence integrity = chain of custody.

4.7.title: Communication & professionalism
4.7.content:
• Empathize, don't argue — for an angry customer, project a positive attitude and focus on what you can do.
  • Project confidence when stakes are high (lost photos, panicked user) — calm + competent is what they need to hear.
  • Active listening, no interrupting — even when the user is frustrated or wrong. Repeat back what you heard to confirm.
  • Closed questions (yes/no, "did you change anything recently?") — use to take control of a meandering call and establish facts.
  • Open questions — use to gather context ("walk me through what happened").
  • Don't gossip about clients in public — vent privately, in person, with a trusted colleague. Never on social media or a shared channel.
  • Escalate when stuck — exhausted your knowledge? Hand off to a senior tech and tell the customer the next steps.
  • Avoid jargon with non-technical users.
  • Cultural sensitivity, punctuality, dress for the environment.

For the exam: Angry user → empathize. Stuck → escalate with next steps for the customer. Need to vent → face-to-face with a colleague, not online.

4.8.title: Scripting basics
4.8.content:
ExtensionLanguage / use
.bat / .cmdWindows batch — legacy / lightweight. Useful for mapping drives at login on older Windows.
.ps1PowerShell — modern Windows automation, cmdlets, .NET objects. Right answer for "Windows domain login script."
.vbsVBScript — legacy Windows scripting; mostly deprecated.
.shBash / shell — Linux and macOS.
.pyPython — cross-platform, general-purpose.
.jsJavaScript — primarily for interactive web content; runs in browsers and (via Node) on servers.

Basic concepts

  • Variable — named storage for a value.
  • Loop — repeats a block (e.g. for iterating over a list of IP addresses to ping each).
  • Conditional (if / else) — branch on a condition.
  • Comment — non-executed note (# in PowerShell / Python / Bash; REM or :: in batch).

Risks of running unknown scripts

  • Unintended system changes, removal of files, accidental privilege escalation, malware delivery. Review code before execution; restrict execution policy on PowerShell (Set-ExecutionPolicy).

For the exam: "Windows login automation" → .bat (legacy) or .ps1 (modern). "Web-page interactive content" → JavaScript.

4.9.title: Remote access technologies
4.9.content:
ProtocolWhat / when
RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol)Microsoft. Full GUI control of a remote Windows machine. Default TCP 3389.
VNC (Virtual Network Computing)Cross-platform GUI remote control. Right answer for Windows ↔ Linux GUI sessions.
SSH (Secure Shell)Encrypted command-line access. Default TCP 22. The standard for Linux / macOS / network device admin.
TelnetLegacy plaintext CLI. Don't use — credentials in cleartext.
VPN (Virtual Private Network)Encrypted tunnel into the corporate network from outside. The user gets a virtual presence inside the LAN — accesses file shares, internal apps. Doesn't give desktop control on its own.
RMM (Remote Monitoring and Management)Centralized platform for IT to monitor, manage, and push automated updates to many client endpoints. Right answer when scale is "hundreds of devices simultaneously."
MSRA / Quick AssistOne-off Windows helper sessions for a non-technical user; they generate a code and read it to support.

For the exam: "Work from home, need network access only" → VPN. "Take over a remote Linux desktop from Windows" → VNC. "Manage hundreds of endpoints, push updates" → RMM.

4.10.title: Using AI tools responsibly (new in 220-1202)
4.10.content:
The 2025 Core 2 objectives add generative-AI awareness. Expect questions on the risks.

  • Hallucination — an AI confidently generates false or fabricated information (fake facts, citations, events). Always verify AI output against authoritative sources.
  • Data privacy / leakage — don't feed sensitive or proprietary data into public AI tools; the provider may use your input for training, exposing it to others.
  • Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) — submitting AI-generated work as your own can violate plagiarism / academic-integrity rules. Follow the org's AUP on AI use.
  • Bias & accuracy — models reflect their training data; output can be biased or out of date.

For the exam: confidently-wrong AI output = a hallucination; pasting company secrets into a public chatbot = a data-leakage / privacy risk.
